strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a timely and potentially useful direction—a single mask-based discrete-diffusion backbone for understanding and generation across text, images, and speech. Extending Dream-7B with modality vocabularies and a progressive multimodal training pipeline is an interesting systems contribution.

Soundness: The model is evaluated across several task families, including ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, and speech-to-image. The reported results show competitive VQA performance and improvements over the older AnyGPT baseline on the evaluated speech tasks.

Presentation: The architecture, three-stage training pipeline, and inference heuristics are described clearly at a high level. The figures and tables are legible, and the qualitative examples help communicate the intended capabilities.

The ability to perform image inpainting through masked-token conditioning without task-specific fine-tuning is a promising consequence of the formulation, although it is demonstrated only qualitatively.
weaknesses: Soundness: None of the central proposed components is ablated. There is no controlled evidence for the benefits of attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, adaptive token-length assignment, the three-stage curriculum, or the SDVI dataset. Consequently, the paper does not establish which contributions cause the reported performance or whether the heuristics improve over straightforward alternatives.

The claimed unified joint distribution over discrete text, image, and speech tokens is inconsistent with the described architecture. Speech input is processed by SenseVoiceSmall into continuous representations and projected through an MLP, whereas speech output uses discrete GLM-4-Voice tokens. Thus, the system does not appear to model one shared joint distribution over the same discrete speech variables in both directions, weakening a central conceptual claim.

The evidence does not substantiate the broad “any-to-any” claim. Quantitative evaluation covers only a small subset of modality directions, while image-plus-speech-to-speech interaction is supported by two qualitative examples. There is no quantitative evaluation of spoken visual interaction, image-to-speech, real-speech-to-image robustness, or more general combinations of the three modalities.

The efficiency claim is inadequately evaluated. Table 3 reports quality as the number of diffusion steps changes but provides no wall-clock latency, throughput, memory, FLOPs, hardware setting, or comparison with autoregressive decoding. Because every diffusion step processes the sequence and TTS still uses a number of steps proportional to sequence length, fewer steps alone do not demonstrate practical speed advantages.

Several conclusions overstate the numerical evidence. Omni-Diffusion's LibriSpeech WER is 7.05 versus 2.82 for GLM-4-Voice, so it is not comparable to the listed specialized speech result; its TTS WER of 3.07 is also worse than CosyVoice's 2.89. On image generation it trails several visual systems, and comparisons across models are not controlled for training data, tokenizers, or evaluation implementation.

The speech-to-image test uses captions synthesized by CosyVoice2, closely matching the synthetic-speech construction used for SDVI. This does not establish robustness to natural speakers, accents, noise, or recording conditions. The paper also reports no uncertainty, multiple seeds, human evaluation, or perceptual speech-quality metric; TTS is judged only through ASR WER.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Missing details include batch sizes, training steps or epochs, data-mixture weights, compute and hardware, masking/noise and decoding schedules, top-k schedule, classifier-free-guidance and repetition-penalty settings, random seeds, and dataset preprocessing. A 2M-sample in-house VQA dataset is not documented or released, the project link is blank, and no code or checkpoint availability is stated. Table 4 also lists JourneyDB twice with 4M examples, creating ambiguity.

Presentation and positioning need improvement: the paper contains no limitations section, has multiple typographical errors, and does not adequately distinguish its novelty from contemporaneous diffusion multimodal systems such as MMADA, DIMPLE, and Lumina-DiMOO beyond asserting that it is the first any-to-any model.

Research ethics are not addressed. The authors clone voices from 1,000 GigaSpeech samples and train on large web-derived image and speech corpora without discussing speaker consent, licensing, privacy, impersonation or synthetic-speech misuse, dataset bias, safeguards, or generated-content provenance. These concerns are material for a speech-generating system, although they could be addressed through a proper ethics and data-governance discussion.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a timely and potentially useful direction—replacing an autoregressive backbone with masked discrete diffusion in a unified text-image-speech system. Integrating understanding and generation within one 7B backbone is an ambitious systems contribution.

Soundness: The model demonstrates nontrivial capability across ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, and image inpainting. Some reported results are competitive, including 34.5 on SEED-2-Plus and 3.07 TTS WER on LibriTTS.

Presentation: The architecture, three-stage training pipeline, and inference heuristics are explained clearly at a high level, and the paper includes useful qualitative examples and a dataset summary.

The study examines reduced-step decoding: image CLIP scores degrade only modestly from 256 to 10 steps, providing preliminary evidence that masked parallel decoding may be useful for multimodal generation.
weaknesses: Soundness: None of the paper's principal technical choices is ablated. There is no controlled evidence for the three-stage curriculum, SDVI training data, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, or adaptive length assignment. Consequently, claims that these components improve stability or quality are unsupported.

The central probabilistic formulation is internally unclear. Section 3.1 describes a joint distribution over discrete text, image, and speech tokens, but speech input is later described as continuous SenseVoice representations projected through an MLP, whereas speech output uses a different GLM-4-Voice tokenizer. Most training data are also pairwise rather than text-speech-image triples. Thus, the claimed unified discrete joint model and 'intrinsically aligned semantic representation space' are not established.

The 'any-to-any' claim substantially exceeds the evaluation. Quantitative results cover only ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, and synthesized-speech-to-image. Image-plus-speech-to-speech is represented only by two qualitative transcripts, with no audio available for assessment; other modality directions and combinations are not tested.

The comparisons do not convincingly establish parity with existing systems. Omni-Diffusion's ASR WER is 7.05 versus 2.82 for GLM-4-Voice, contrary to the text's characterization of comparable performance. Text-to-image evaluation uses only CLIP-T/CLIP-I, where the method is not consistently strongest, without FID, human preference, compositionality, or prompt-following evaluation. TTS is assessed only through ASR-derived WER, omitting naturalness, speaker similarity, prosody, and human evaluation.

The efficiency conclusion is unsupported by actual efficiency measurements. Reporting denoising-step counts does not establish lower latency or higher throughput than autoregressive systems; no wall-clock timing, hardware, memory, batch-size scaling, or quality-matched baseline is provided. Moreover, TTS still uses a number of iterations proportional to sequence length.

The speech-to-image test uses captions synthesized by CosyVoice2, the same synthesizer used to construct SDVI training data. This narrow synthetic-speech setting does not establish robustness to real speakers, accents, noise, or spontaneous speech. No contamination or overlap analysis is reported for the large web-derived training corpora and evaluation benchmarks.

Originality: The overall recipe largely combines an existing diffusion LM, pretrained modality tokenizers/encoders/decoders, standard masked-token training, and heuristic inference modifications. Closely related diffusion multimodal systems such as MMaDA, Dimple, and Lumina-DiMOO are cited, but the distinctions are not experimentally isolated; this also makes the unqualified 'first' claim difficult to sustain.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The project-page field is blank, and no code or checkpoints are supplied. Missing details include compute and hardware, batch sizes, training duration or update counts, sampling/masking schedules, top-k schedule, classifier-free-guidance and repetition-penalty settings, dataset mixing weights, preprocessing, evaluation prompts, random seeds, uncertainty, and benchmark splits. The 2M-sample in-house VQA dataset is undocumented, and Table 4 appears to duplicate JourneyDB as two separate 4M entries.

Presentation contains several consequential ambiguities and errors, including categorical token sequences declared as elements of R^L, an undefined mapping from diffusion time to mask ratio, unclear position-penalty notation, and no explanation of how token types and variable multimodal sequence layouts are represented. Qualitative image examples are few and potentially cherry-picked, while spoken outputs are shown only as text transcriptions.

Limitations and ethics are essentially absent. The manuscript does not discuss voice-cloning consent and impersonation risks, licensing and privacy of GigaSpeech/LAION-derived data, biases across accents and languages, harmful image or speech generation, hallucinations, safeguards, dataset-release conditions, or the environmental cost of training. Given the use of cloned voices and large web corpora, this is a material omission.

Overall, the manuscript presents a promising prototype, but its central claims about unified joint modeling, component effectiveness, any-to-any coverage, and efficiency are not supported by sufficiently controlled or comprehensive evidence. These are acceptance-blocking issues rather than minor revision points. strengths: The manuscript presents an ambitious unified 7B masked-discrete-diffusion system that directly models text, image, and speech tokens within one backbone; this is a useful and reasonably original exploration of an alternative to autoregressive multimodal models. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/5543ef6c457d43569864e583c249cc20/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The system covers an unusually broad range of tasks, including ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken visual interaction, and training-free image inpainting. This breadth supports the significance of the overall research direction.

The proposed progressive training pipeline, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, special-token pre-infilling, and adaptive output-length initialization are technically plausible adaptations to masked diffusion.

Reported results are promising: the model improves over AnyGPT on ASR, is close to CosyVoice on TTS WER, reaches 1216.7 MME-P and 34.5 Seed-2-Plus, and retains much of its image-generation quality when reducing sampling from 256 to 10 steps.
The paper is generally well organized, and its architecture, training stages, decoding process, datasets, and principal hyperparameters are described clearly enough to understand the approach.
weaknesses: Soundness is limited by the complete absence of component-wise ablations. The manuscript introduces several central techniques but does not isolate the effects of progressive training, attenuated tail-pad masking, position penalty, pre-infilling, or adaptive length assignment. Consequently, the evidence does not establish which innovations are necessary or whether the unified formulation itself drives the gains.

The evaluation does not fully substantiate the headline any-to-any and unified-alignment claims. There is no quantitative evaluation of tri-modal spoken visual interaction, only two small qualitative examples; no evaluation of the retained text capability; and no broad cross-modal transfer analysis. Speech-to-image evaluation merely converts COCO captions to synthetic speech with CosyVoice2, closely resembling the constructed training pipeline.

Generation evaluation is narrow. CLIP-T and CLIP-I alone are insufficient to establish text-to-image quality, while TTS is evaluated only through ASR-derived WER, which does not measure naturalness, intelligibility to humans, speaker similarity, prosody, or audio artifacts. No human evaluation, MOS, FID, GenEval-style compositional evaluation, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests are reported.

The claimed efficiency advantage is not actually measured end to end. Table 3 reports quality versus numbers of diffusion steps but gives no latency, throughput, memory use, hardware-normalized comparison, or comparison against autoregressive baselines. Parallel decoding can still be slower in wall-clock terms, so the efficiency conclusion is presently unsupported.

Several comparisons and claims are overstated or potentially unfair. Omni-Diffusion's 7.05 ASR WER is far behind GLM-4-Voice's 2.82, and its 3.07 TTS WER is slightly worse than CosyVoice's 2.89. Parameter counts apparently omit modality tokenizers/encoders/decoders, while some baselines are marked as using external models. Recent omni-modal systems cited by the paper are not empirically compared.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a resource-intensive systems paper. The appendix omits batch sizes, training steps or epochs, compute and hardware, stage-wise dataset sampling ratios, random seeds, most decoding/CFG/repetition settings, and checkpoint or code-release details. Table 4 also contains duplicated JourneyDB entries, a likely incorrect Common Voice citation, and an unexplained 2M-sample in-house dataset.

Originality is promising but the claim of being the first such model needs more careful qualification given closely related masked-diffusion multimodal work such as MMaDA, DIMPLE, and Lumina-DiMOO, as well as NExT-Omni. The core objective is a straightforward masked-token cross-entropy formulation; the main novelty lies in system integration and heuristics rather than a new diffusion method.

The paper contains no dedicated limitations or ethics discussion. This is material because training uses large web-scale and in-house datasets plus voice cloning from 1,000 GigaSpeech samples. Dataset licensing, consent, privacy, speaker impersonation risks, harmful image or speech generation, demographic bias, and safeguards are not addressed. Overall, the idea and initial results are compelling, but the missing controls and incomplete validation prevent reliable acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality/significance: The paper explores a timely and potentially valuable direction—using masked discrete diffusion as the backbone of a text-image-speech system rather than defaulting to autoregressive modeling. The unified 7B backbone, progressive training pipeline, and demonstrations of speech-to-image and spoken visual interaction constitute a meaningful systems contribution.

Soundness: The reported breadth is promising. Omni-Diffusion is evaluated on ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image generation, speech-to-image generation, spoken VQA, inpainting, and sampling efficiency. It is competitive with the selected any-to-any baselines; examples include POPE 76.6, MME-P 1216.7, Seed-2-Plus 34.5, and lower ASR WER than AnyGPT.

The sampling study usefully exposes quality-efficiency tradeoffs rather than reporting only one operating point. Text-to-image latency decreases from 28.57 seconds at 256 steps to 1.29 seconds at 10 steps, with a corresponding CLIP-I decrease from 0.667 to 0.650.

Presentation: The overall architecture and three-stage training process are clearly motivated and illustrated. The paper distinguishes masked diffusion from discrete flow matching and generally organizes the method and experiments coherently.
The appendix provides dataset quantities and several optimization hyperparameters, while the qualitative figures show visually plausible text-to-image, speech-to-image, and inpainting behavior.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central claim of learning a joint distribution over discrete text, image, and speech tokens is not adequately reconciled with the architecture description. Speech input is processed by SenseVoiceSmall into continuous representations and projected through an MLP, whereas speech output uses discrete GLM-4-Voice tokens. The paper does not formally explain how these continuous input representations fit Eq. (1), the purported single discrete vocabulary, or the claimed joint discrete distribution.

The claimed benefits of the proposed techniques are largely unsupported by ablations. There are no controlled ablations for attenuated tail-pad masking, the three-stage curriculum, SDVI training, or adaptive token-length assignment. Special-token pre-infilling is supported only by two qualitative examples. The position penalty changes CLIP-T from 0.233 to 0.235 and CLIP-I from 0.666 to 0.667, without variance estimates, repeated runs, or evidence that the difference is significant.

The any-to-any claim is stronger than the evaluation. Only a limited subset of modality mappings is quantitatively tested, and genuinely trimodal interaction is evaluated mainly on an MME variant whose questions were synthesized by the same CosyVoice2 family used during data construction. Performance also falls substantially from 1216.7 for text-plus-image input to 1019.9 for speech-plus-image input and 1004.6 for speech output.

Speech evaluation is insufficient. TTS is judged only through Whisper transcription WER, which does not measure naturalness, intelligibility to humans, prosody, speaker similarity, or audio artifacts. Moreover, Omni-Diffusion's TTS WER of 3.07 is worse than CosyVoice's 2.89, contrary to the table caption's statement that it is superior to specialized speech models. ASR WER of 7.05 is also far behind GLM-4-Voice's 2.82.

The comparisons do not convincingly isolate the proposed diffusion backbone. Omni-Diffusion relies on strong pretrained Dream-7B, MAGViT-v2, SenseVoiceSmall, and GLM-4-Voice components, but component parameters and their contribution are not accounted for. Baselines differ in training data, external decoders, model size, and evaluation provenance; several entries are copied from prior work while others are rerun.

The efficiency claim lacks a controlled comparison. Hardware, precision, batch size, compilation settings, warm-up, and whether tokenization or modality decoding is included are not reported. Latencies against autoregressive baselines therefore are not directly interpretable, and the fastest operating points trade away measurable quality.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The project-webpage field is blank, no code or checkpoint is provided, and essential details are missing: training steps or epochs, compute resources, modality sampling ratios, exact masking schedule, pad-length distribution, optimizer schedule, classifier-free-guidance scale, repetition penalty, decoding schedule, random seeds, and evaluation prompts. A 2M-sample in-house dataset is undocumented; Table 4 duplicates a 4M JourneyDB entry and incorrectly cites Common Voice 17 with the LibriSpeech reference.

Presentation contains consequential inconsistencies beyond minor copy-editing. The manuscript alternates between discrete speech tokens and continuous speech-encoder features, calls the system 'built entirely' or 'purely' on masked diffusion despite using modality-specific pretrained encoders and decoders, and defines x0 as an element of R^L despite treating it as a discrete sequence.

Limitations and ethics are treated inadequately. The limitation section is essentially a single future-work statement and omits the narrow English-centric evaluation, synthetic-speech dependence, comparison limitations, computational cost, and possible failure modes. The generic impact statement does not address voice-cloning consent and impersonation, deepfake or image-generation misuse, speaker privacy, dataset licensing, demographic bias, or safeguards. These concerns are especially material because SDVI explicitly clones 1,000 sampled GigaSpeech voices.

Overall, the architectural direction is promising, but unsupported central claims, incomplete evaluations and ablations, weak reproducibility, and insufficient ethical analysis prevent acceptance in its current form. Substantial additional evidence and clarification would be required before others could reliably build on the contribution.

strengths: Originality/significance: Extending a pretrained masked discrete-diffusion language model into a single 7B system spanning text, image, and speech is a timely and potentially useful research direction. The ability to perform understanding and generation with one backbone, including speech-conditioned image generation and training-free image inpainting, is appealing.

Methodology: The progressive three-stage training pipeline is intuitively motivated, and the paper proposes several diffusion-specific mechanisms—attenuated tail-pad masking, position-penalized image decoding, special-token pre-infilling, and adaptive output-length initialization.

Empirical breadth: The evaluation covers ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image generation, speech-to-image generation, spoken VQA, inpainting, and decoding latency. The reported results are sometimes competitive with prior any-to-any systems; for example, POPE/MME/Seed-2-Plus results exceed the listed any-to-any baselines where comparisons are available.

Presentation: The overall architecture and training stages are explained clearly, with readable diagrams, qualitative examples, and a useful summary of training datasets and major optimization hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Soundness: The broad central claims are not supported by sufficiently rigorous evidence. “Any-to-any” capability is demonstrated only through a limited subset of modality mappings, with no systematic evaluation of all input-output combinations, multi-turn interaction, ordinary text generation, or preservation of the pretrained language model's capabilities. The claimed intrinsically aligned shared semantic space is asserted rather than directly analyzed.

Soundness: Speech input is described as continuous SenseVoice representations projected through an MLP, whereas the probabilistic formulation treats speech as discrete tokens and claims unified modeling of the joint distribution of discrete multimodal tokens. Speech encoding and generation also use different pretrained components. This makes the claimed fully unified discrete formulation materially less clear than presented.

Evaluation quality: Several conclusions overstate the tables. The paper calls ASR performance “comparable” to specialized models although its 7.05 WER is much worse than GLM-4-Voice's 2.82. TTS is evaluated only through ASR-derived WER, without naturalness, intelligibility, speaker similarity, prosody, or human evaluation. Image generation relies heavily on CLIP similarities and a small set of curated examples, while spoken interaction has almost no perceptual evaluation.

Evaluation quality: Speech-to-image and spoken-VQA tests synthesize their speech using CosyVoice2, the same synthesizer used to construct the SDVI training data. This creates a substantial matched-synthesizer bias and does not establish robustness to real speakers, accents, noise, spontaneous speech, or alternative TTS systems.

Baselines and efficiency: Table 2 is sparse and compares against heterogeneous, often older systems with many missing metrics. The latency comparisons omit hardware, precision, batch size, compilation, and whether tokenizer/decoder costs are included, so the efficiency claim is not reproducible or demonstrably fair. The full 256-step image sampler is substantially slower than the reported autoregressive baselines, while the 10-step setting trades away quality.

Ablations: The proposed contributions are inadequately isolated. Position penalty yields only 0.002 CLIP-T and 0.001 CLIP-I improvements, with no uncertainty or repeated runs. Special-token pre-infilling receives only two qualitative examples. There are no convincing controlled ablations for attenuated tail-pad masking, the three-stage curriculum, SDVI training, or adaptive length assignment, and no evidence for the hypothesized cause of repetitive image patterns.

Reproducibility: Essential details are absent, including training steps or epochs, modality sampling ratios, masking schedule, optimizer schedule, top-k decoding schedule, classifier-free guidance and repetition-penalty values, random seeds, hardware and compute, and detailed evaluation protocols. The project-page field is empty, no code or checkpoint availability is stated, and a 2M-sample in-house dataset is undocumented. Table 4 also lists JourneyDB twice with 4M samples, leaving the training mixture ambiguous.

Presentation: Although readable, the paper contains imprecise or inconsistent descriptions and numerous language errors. More importantly, it repeatedly generalizes from narrow results—for example, from synthetic speech experiments to “strong alignment across various modalities” and from qualitative inpainting examples to an advantage over autoregressive models.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section is only one short paragraph about adding future tasks and does not acknowledge the evaluation, synthetic-speech, compute, data, or generalization limitations above. The impact statement dismisses all societal consequences despite voice cloning and general-purpose image/speech generation. It does not discuss impersonation and deepfake misuse, speaker consent, privacy, bias, harmful generation, dataset licensing, the in-house data source, or safeguards. These omissions are material for a system with speech cloning and multimodal generation capabilities.

strengths: Originality: The paper presents a novel and timely attempt to use a masked discrete-diffusion backbone for unified text, image, and speech understanding and generation, rather than attaching separate generative models to an autoregressive LLM.

Significance: A single 7B model supporting ASR, TTS, VQA, text-to-image, speech-to-image, spoken visual interaction, and zero-shot image inpainting is an ambitious and potentially useful contribution.

Soundness: The model is evaluated across multiple established benchmarks. Particularly encouraging results include 34.5 on Seed-2-Plus, competitive MME-P performance, TTS WER of 3.07, and similar image-generation metrics for text and synthesized-speech conditioning.

The progressive training pipeline and diffusion-specific inference mechanisms are intuitively motivated. The latency-quality results in Tables 3, 8, and 9 also provide useful evidence that parallel decoding can yield practical speed advantages at reduced step counts.

Presentation: The manuscript has a clear high-level narrative, helpful architecture and training diagrams, readable tables, and generally polished visual presentation. The qualitative generations are diverse and visually convincing.
weaknesses: Soundness: The ablations do not adequately support the proposed technical components. The position penalty changes CLIP-T only from 0.233 to 0.235 and CLIP-I from 0.666 to 0.667, without uncertainty or significance analysis; special-token pre-infilling is supported by only two qualitative examples; and there are no controlled ablations for attenuated tail-pad masking, the three-stage curriculum, SDVI training, or adaptive token-length assignment.

Several claims overstate the evidence. ASR WER is 7.05 versus 2.82 for GLM-4-Voice, while TTS WER is 3.07 versus 2.89 for CosyVoice, so the characterization of broadly comparable or superior speech performance is not fully justified. Likewise, the claimed intrinsically aligned shared representation space is inferred from downstream results rather than directly analyzed.

The efficiency comparison is insufficiently controlled: hardware, precision, batch size, implementation optimizations, and baseline measurement conditions are not reported. The strongest 256-step setting takes 28.5 seconds per image, and the faster 10-step setting sacrifices quality, making the broad efficiency conclusion difficult to assess.

Originality is meaningful at the system level but less clear at the component level. The training curriculum and inference techniques are mostly heuristic extensions of existing masked-diffusion practices, and comparison with the closest contemporary discrete-flow/diffusion multimodal systems, including NeXT-Omni and Lumina-DiMOO, is missing despite their discussion in the paper.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript omits training duration or steps per stage, compute resources, data-mixture ratios, masking and decoding schedules, top-k schedules, classifier-free-guidance and repetition-penalty settings, and several preprocessing details. The project-page field is blank, and 2M samples come from an undocumented in-house dataset. Table 4 also appears to list JourneyDB twice, creating ambiguity about the training mixture.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish general any-to-any capability: some modality mappings receive only qualitative examples, Spoken VQA uses questions synthesized by the same TTS family used in training-data construction, and there is no evaluation on real noisy speech, diverse speakers, human judgments of speech quality, or systematic tests of cross-modal consistency.

Limitations and ethics are treated too superficially. The limitations section mentions only future visual editing, while the system raises risks involving synthetic speech and images, voice cloning from 1,000 GigaSpeech samples, consent and licensing, impersonation and misinformation, demographic bias, and harmful multimodal generation. Data provenance and safeguards are not discussed. Overall, the core idea is promising, but the missing controlled evidence and reproducibility details currently prevent others from reliably validating and building on it.
